questions.topic: What is the difference between var, let, and const
questions.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const? Explain scope, hoisting, and reassignment.

definition.text: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped bindings.

motivation.whyIntroduced: JavaScript originally exposed var for local declarations. let and const were added in ES2015 to provide block scoping and clearer rebinding intent, avoiding bugs from accidental redeclaration and loops sharing a binding.
motivation.historicalNote: This describes the underlying engineering motivation, not a claim about a single inventor or release.

problemSolved.before: A var declared inside an if or for block can remain visible outside that block, and redeclaration is allowed in the same scope.
problemSolved.after: let and const establish block-level bindings; const prevents reassignment of that binding, while let permits reassignment.

characteristics: var: function-scoped (or global when declared at top level of a script)
let: block-scoped and reassignable
const: block-scoped and not reassignable
All declarations are processed before execution, but let/const cannot be accessed before initialization (temporal dead zone)
const protects the binding, not the contents of a referenced object

simpleAnalogy.title: Labels on containers
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Think of var as a label usable anywhere in a room (function), while let and const labels live inside a smaller marked area (block). A const label cannot be moved to another container, but the contents of its current container may still change.

industryExample.scenario: A transaction table iterates over results and creates click handlers to open each transaction.
industryExample.implementation: Use const for each transaction identifier within an iteration, so every handler captures the intended row; keep a variable let when the UI genuinely needs to reassign a selection.
industryExample.businessImpact: Avoids selecting the wrong transaction from an asynchronously used callback.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Correct authorization and transaction access must still be checked by the server.

useCases: Default to const for values whose bindings do not change
Use let for counters or variables intentionally reassigned
Use block scope to isolate temporary results
Recognize var in legacy Angular/JavaScript codebases

steps: A list of transactions is rendered
Each item gets a block-scoped identifier
The click callback closes over that identifier
A later click logs or routes to the correct transaction
Backend independently checks authorization for that identifier

diagrams.title: Concept and business flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[Transaction list] --> B[For each transaction]
    B --> C[Create const transactionId]
    C --> D[Create click handler]
    D --> E[User clicks row later]
    E --> F[Correct transaction ID selected]
diagrams.caption: Conceptual model; precise runtime behavior is explained in the accompanying steps.

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript 5+ compiled for modern JavaScript / Node.js 20+
explanation: const transactionId is a new binding for each iteration
Every callback retains the correct iteration binding
let selectedId expresses legitimate rebinding
A const object remains mutable unless separately frozen or typed read-only

projectExperience.example: In a banking transaction-list feature, I would prefer const bindings for transaction IDs inside event handlers and let only for values that are intentionally reassigned.
evidenceToCollect: A test proving the correct row opens after asynchronous interaction
A pull request showing consistent lint rules
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Do not say you implemented this in production unless you actually did.

pitfalls: var loop variables may cause callbacks to observe the same final variable
let and const have a temporal dead zone before declaration initialization
Top-level var in a classic script differs from top-level declarations in ES modules
const does not deeply freeze arrays or objects
Switching a legacy var to const can break code that intentionally reassigns it
whenNotToUse: Do not use var for new application code unless preserving an intentional legacy behavior
Do not use const when a binding must be reassigned
Do not equate const with immutable data; use immutable update patterns or Object.freeze as appropriate

alternatives.name: Object.freeze or readonly typing
alternatives.bestFor: Communicating or enforcing restrictions on object mutation
alternatives.tradeoff: Object.freeze is shallow by default; TypeScript readonly is compile-time only

alternatives.name: let
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires discipline to avoid accidental rebinding

testing.strategy: Run examples and assert scope, callback and mutation behavior.

testCases.expected: First handler returns tx-1 and second returns tx-2
let can be reassigned while reassigning const is rejected

negativeCases: Redeclaring let in one block is a syntax error

beginner: Why can a const object still be mutated?
intermediate: Why did var cause unexpected callbacks in older for loops?
advanced: How do closures and module scope interact with Angular component instances?
expert: How would you gradually migrate a large legacy JavaScript application to consistent declaration rules?

answer.finalTakeaway: Prefer const; use let for rebinding; avoid var in new code.

questions.topic: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript
questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?

definition.text: === compares without coercion; == may convert operands before comparison.

motivation.whyIntroduced: JavaScript supports loose equality for interoperability among values of different types, while strict equality provides a more predictable comparison that avoids implicit conversions.
motivation.historicalNote: This describes the underlying engineering motivation, not a claim about a single inventor or release.

problemSolved.before: Loose equality can make unrelated-looking values compare equal after coercion, such as the number 0 and the string "0".
problemSolved.after: Strict equality compares using the language’s strict equality semantics without coercing operand types.

characteristics: === does not coerce different operand types
== follows abstract equality conversion rules
NaN is unequal to itself under either operator
Objects are compared by reference identity under both operators
null == undefined is true; null === undefined is false

simpleAnalogy.title: Checking badges
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A loose check may treat a badge numbered 7 and a badge labeled "7" as interchangeable; a strict check requires the actual kind of badge and value to align.

industryExample.scenario: A shopping cart holds a numeric product ID while a route parameter arrives as a string.
industryExample.implementation: Parse and validate the route parameter into the expected type, then use === rather than relying on implicit == conversion.
industryExample.businessImpact: Avoids silently matching malformed or unexpectedly typed identifiers.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Regardless of client comparisons, the backend must validate ownership, prices and order data.

useCases: Comparing validated IDs of the same type
Checking for an explicitly undefined value

steps: Angular router supplies a route parameter as text
Validate the text as a well-formed numeric identifier
Convert it to the domain’s number type
Find the product with strict equality
Server independently validates the product on checkout

diagrams.title: Concept and business flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A[Route param as string] --> B{Valid numeric ID?}
    B -->|No| C[Show invalid request]
    B -->|Yes| D[Convert to number]
    D --> E[Compare with ===]
    E --> F[Display matching product]
diagrams.caption: Conceptual model; precise runtime behavior is explained in the accompanying steps.

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript 5+ compiled for modern JavaScript / Node.js 20+
explanation: The route parameter is validated before conversion
Strict equality compares numbers with numbers
An invalid identifier yields no selected product rather than accidental matching
The == line is a demonstration, not a recommendation

projectExperience.example: In an e-commerce product details route, I would validate the product ID type before searching cached product models with strict equality.
evidenceToCollect: Unit tests for invalid, missing and valid product IDs
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Do not represent this as previous work unless completed.

pitfalls: 0 == false is true but 0 === false is false
A pair of distinct object literals never compare equal by identity
NaN is not equal to itself; Number.isNaN detects it
null and undefined compare equal under ==
Number(" ") becomes 0, so conversion must be validated
whenNotToUse: Do not assume === performs deep equality for arrays or objects
Do not use === alone to validate untrusted external input

alternatives.name: Object.is
alternatives.tradeoff: Slightly different semantics from strict equality

alternatives.name: Deep comparison
alternatives.bestFor: Comparing object structure when truly necessary
alternatives.tradeoff: More expensive and requires clear semantics

testing.strategy: Check boundaries where external strings are converted to domain types.

testCases.expected: Different object instances are not equal under ===

negativeCases: Whitespace should not become an accepted zero identifier
null should not match undefined with ===

advanced: Why is reference equality important in UI state updates?
expert: How would you enforce ID normalization at API boundaries in a large application?

answer.finalTakeaway: Normalize external values, then compare strictly and deliberately.

questions.question: What are closures in JavaScript? Demonstrate a real use case.

definition.text: A closure retains access to its surrounding lexical variables.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Closures arise naturally from lexical scoping and first-class functions. They make it possible for callbacks and returned functions to keep using values from the scope where they were defined after that scope has returned.
motivation.historicalNote: This describes the underlying engineering motivation, not a claim about a single inventor or release.

problemSolved.before: A callback may need configuration or private state that is not passed as an argument whenever it runs.
problemSolved.after: A function captures access to its lexical environment, allowing later calls to use that configuration or state.
benefits: State can remain private without global variables

characteristics: Closures capture bindings rather than frozen snapshots
Captured variables can change between calls
Each factory invocation can create independent state
A closure may extend the lifetime of captured objects
Closures occur in event handlers, subscriptions and callbacks

simpleAnalogy.title: A labeled locker
simpleAnalogy.explanation: You receive a key to a locker containing a counter. Even after the receptionist leaves, the key still accesses the same locker; a different visitor can receive a key to a different locker.

industryExample.scenario: A shipment dashboard creates a status filter for one carrier without showing other carriers’ shipments.
industryExample.implementation: Use a function factory that captures a carrier ID to create a reusable filtering predicate for the appropriate UI data.
industryExample.businessImpact: Keeps the filter logic readable and scoped to the selected carrier.
industryExample.importantConstraint: This is only a UI filter; backend authorization must enforce carrier data separation.

useCases: Factory functions for formatters and validators

steps: Carrier ID arrives from a selected filter
A filter factory receives the carrier ID
It returns a function closing over that ID
A shipment array is filtered by the returned function
Only the matching UI rows are shown; server authorization is independent

diagrams.title: Concept and business flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[Select carrier C-1] --> B[makeCarrierFilter C-1]
    B --> C[Closure retains carrierId]
    C --> D[Shipments.filter predicate]
    D --> E[Matching rows rendered]
diagrams.caption: Conceptual model; precise runtime behavior is explained in the accompanying steps.

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript 5+ compiled for modern JavaScript / Node.js 20+
explanation: The returned predicate retains access to the carrierId binding
Counter factory calls create separate closure environments
No global count is needed
The filtered data is presentation logic; it is not authorization

projectExperience.example: In a logistics dashboard, I would create carrier-specific filter predicates using closures and separately enforce carrier permissions in the tracking API.
evidenceToCollect: Unit tests for separate carrier filter instances
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a suggested implementation, not a claim about your past projects.

pitfalls: Closure does not freeze captured state; changing an outer variable changes observed values
Long-lived event handlers can retain large objects and cause memory pressure
var loop captures can unexpectedly share one binding
Closures can hide state in ways that make debugging harder
UI filtering cannot provide access control
whenNotToUse: Do not use a closure when plain function arguments are clearer
Do not capture entire large objects in long-lived callbacks unnecessarily
Do not treat a client-side closure as a security boundary

alternatives.name: Explicit function arguments
alternatives.tradeoff: Caller must pass context each time

alternatives.name: Class or object instance
alternatives.bestFor: Complex stateful behavior with an explicit API

testing.strategy: Verify independence, captured state and memory cleanup.

testCases.expected: Only s1 and s3 are returned
Incrementing one does not increment another

negativeCases: Changing a captured let binding affects later invocations
Removing UI filter does not grant backend access

beginner: What happens to local variables after their function returns when a closure retains them?
intermediate: What is the difference between closure capture with var and let in a loop?
advanced: How can closures contribute to memory leaks in Angular subscriptions?
expert: How would you investigate retained closures in heap snapshots of a long-running dashboard?

answer.finalTakeaway: Closures retain lexical context; use them intentionally and clean up callbacks.

questions.topic: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript
questions.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript? Explain the event loop at a basic level.

definition.text: Synchronous work blocks execution; asynchronous work resumes through scheduled callbacks.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Browser and server programs must handle timers, network activity and user interactions without blocking the JavaScript execution thread while waiting for I/O. Scheduling APIs and event-loop processing allow that cooperation.
motivation.historicalNote: This describes the underlying engineering motivation, not a claim about a single inventor or release.

problemSolved.before: A synchronous wait for a network response would freeze UI work and prevent handling input while the wait lasts.
problemSolved.after: An asynchronous operation initiates work, returns control, and later schedules continuation when a result or event becomes available.
benefits: Ability to handle independent activities without blocking on network latency

characteristics: Synchronous statements run to completion on the current call stack
Promise reactions run as microtasks after the current synchronous stack
Timers usually schedule later tasks rather than execute at an exact time
Microtasks drain before the event loop proceeds to another task in typical browser scheduling
Long CPU-bound JavaScript still blocks the main thread even when invoked from a callback

simpleAnalogy.title: A single cashier
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A cashier can start a ticket for an item that needs preparation, serve other customers meanwhile, and finish that ticket when the result arrives. But a long calculation done directly at the register still blocks the line.

industryExample.scenario: A scheduling screen loads available clinician slots while remaining responsive to user interactions.
industryExample.implementation: The app requests slots asynchronously, displays a loading state, and updates the UI after the response without blocking keystrokes and clicks.
industryExample.businessImpact: Users can navigate and interact while data is fetched.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Asynchronous fetching does not make backend processing faster or guarantee a slot remains available.

useCases: HTTP calls and UI loading states
Managing retries and cancellations at the appropriate layer

steps: The UI starts with an empty availability state
HTTP request begins asynchronously
JavaScript returns control so users can interact
The HTTP result eventually schedules a continuation
State updates and Angular renders the available appointment slots

diagrams.title: Concept and business flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram

    participant UI as Angular UI
    participant API as Scheduling API
    U->>UI: Open schedule
    UI->>API: GET /slots
    Note over UI: UI stays responsive
    API-->>UI: Available slots
    UI-->>U: Render slots
diagrams.caption: Conceptual model; precise runtime behavior is explained in the accompanying steps.

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript 5+ compiled for modern JavaScript / Node.js 20+
explanation: Synchronous logs A and B execute before later callbacks
Promise .then is a microtask; setTimeout callback runs as a later task
await suspends only its async function, not the whole JavaScript thread
Actual order relative to other platform events depends on environment and scheduling

projectExperience.example: In a clinician scheduling page, I would show a loading indicator, request slot data asynchronously, and handle errors without freezing the interface.
evidenceToCollect: A browser performance recording showing responsive input
A test covering loading and error states
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Do not assert performance measurements without actually collecting them.

pitfalls: An async function can perform expensive synchronous work before its first await
setTimeout(..., 0) is not an immediate synchronous callback
Too many recursively scheduled microtasks can delay rendering
An unhandled promise rejection can hide failed work
Async responses may arrive out of order and overwrite newer state
whenNotToUse: Do not use busy-wait loops for network completion
Do not assume async automatically moves CPU-intensive calculations off the main thread
Do not assume timer delays are exact deadlines

alternatives.name: Web Worker
alternatives.tradeoff: Message passing, serialization and operational complexity

alternatives.name: RxJS Observable
alternatives.bestFor: Composable streams and cancellable Angular HTTP subscriptions
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires understanding subscription and operator behavior

testing.strategy: Validate observable sequencing and UI states; use DevTools to inspect main-thread blocking.

testCases.expected: Synchronous logs occur before the Promise microtask, which occurs before the timer task in the shown example

negativeCases: Rejected request shows an error state
CPU-heavy synchronous code may freeze UI despite surrounding async functions

beginner: Why does Promise.then run after synchronous console.log?
intermediate: Why can an older API response overwrite a newer search result?
advanced: How would you profile long tasks that block browser input?
expert: How would you design responsive scheduling UIs under slow networks and large data loads?

answer.finalTakeaway: Asynchrony preserves responsiveness, but correctness still requires managing ordering and errors.

questions.topic: Given an array of objects, how would you filter, sort, group, and transform it using map(), filter(), and reduce()
questions.question: Given an array of objects, how would you filter, sort, group, and transform it using map(), filter(), and reduce()?

definition.text: Filter selects, map transforms, reduce accumulates, and sort orders.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Applications frequently receive collections from APIs but need derived views such as filtered transactions, totals and grouped summaries. Array methods offer declarative, composable operations for such transformations.
motivation.historicalNote: This describes the underlying engineering motivation, not a claim about a single inventor or release.

problemSolved.before: Imperative loops often mix selection, transformation and aggregation into one block, making intent and tests less obvious.
problemSolved.after: Use filter to select records, map to reshape them, reduce to accumulate results, and sort to define order.
benefits: Avoided accidental changes to source collections when copying before sort

characteristics: filter returns selected elements in a new array
map returns a new array with transformed values
reduce combines values into a chosen accumulator
sort mutates the original array; use toSorted or copy before sorting
Comparator functions should return negative, zero or positive numbers

simpleAnalogy.title: Sorting laundry
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Filter keeps only blue clothes, sort orders them by size, map converts each item to a label, and reduce counts how many items belong to each size group.

industryExample.scenario: A banking dashboard must show completed debit transactions, newest first, with a total amount and per-category totals.
industryExample.implementation: Filter transactions to completed debits, sort a copied array by posting timestamp, map records to view models, and reduce them to category aggregates.
industryExample.businessImpact: Produces a clear client-side view of already-authorized records.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Use integer minor currency units or a suitable decimal-money representation; do not use floating-point arithmetic for authoritative financial accounting.

steps: Backend returns authorized transaction DTOs
Select completed debit records
Sort newest to oldest without mutating incoming data
Transform records to lightweight view models
Accumulate totals grouped by category
Render summary and transaction rows

diagrams.title: Concept and business flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A[Authorized API records] --> B[filter completed debits]
    B --> C[sort copied records]
    C --> D[map UI rows]
    C --> E[reduce totals by category]
    D --> F[Angular transaction list]
    E --> G[Angular summary cards]
diagrams.caption: Conceptual model; precise runtime behavior is explained in the accompanying steps.

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript 5+ compiled for modern JavaScript / Node.js 20+
explanation: Filtering produces only completed debit rows
Sorting uses a copy so shared API data is not reordered
Grouping reduces into a category-to-total dictionary
Amounts are stored in integer minor units rather than floats
For large collections, move filtering/aggregation server-side or use pagination

projectExperience.example: In a banking transaction dashboard, I would transform API records into display rows and grouped category totals while preserving the original array for other consumers.
evidenceToCollect: Unit tests for sorting and aggregation
Profiler evidence if dataset is large
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Do not claim financial correctness based solely on client totals.

pitfalls: sort mutates its receiver unless a copy or toSorted is used
Comparing date strings is safe only when formats and time zones are normalized
reduce with a mutable accumulator is okay locally but should not mutate the source items
Grouping across multiple currencies without conversion is incorrect
Client-side pagination followed by aggregation only summarizes the loaded page
whenNotToUse: Do not aggregate millions of records on the main thread when a backend query is appropriate
Do not use floating-point totals as the authoritative accounting ledger
Do not mutate shared input arrays with sort when other UI features depend on their original order

alternatives.name: Server aggregation (SQL GROUP BY)
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires an API contract and query optimization

alternatives.name: RxJS/Signals computed derivation
alternatives.tradeoff: Derivation still needs efficient array operations

alternatives.name: toSorted
alternatives.bestFor: Non-mutating array ordering on supported runtimes

testing.strategy: Assert transformations against a small deterministic fixture, then add malformed and scale cases.
negativeCases: Mixed currencies must be separated or converted correctly

beginner: When do you use map instead of filter?
intermediate: How would you build a derived Angular Signal for category totals?
advanced: How would you optimize virtualized tables and server pagination?
expert: How would you design authoritative financial reporting while avoiding inconsistent client projections?

answer.finalTakeaway: Compose array operations for clarity, preserve inputs, and validate domain semantics.
